content: Efforts to integrate health services for HIV and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in hard-to-reach areas, such as Lesotho, have been documented. These initiatives aim to provide comprehensive care for both adults and children. Similarly, in rural Uganda, rapid community-based HIV testing campaigns have been leveraged to address NCDs, demonstrating the potential for dual-purpose health interventions. Studies have evaluated the effectiveness of linking individuals to care for conditions like hypertension following community-based screenings in Uganda. These findings highlight the importance of integrated care models that address both infectious and chronic diseases. Organizations like FHI360 have emphasized the integration of HIV and NCD care, providing resources and guidelines to support such efforts. In the United States, research has shown a significant prevalence of psychiatric disorders and substance use among adults living with HIV. This underscores the need for mental health services as part of comprehensive HIV care. Meta-analyses have established a strong association between HIV infection and an increased risk of depressive disorders. Depression, in turn, has been linked to poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART), which can compromise treatment outcomes. In sub-Saharan Africa, depression and alcohol use have been identified as barriers to ART adherence. Systematic reviews have highlighted the need for interventions that address these mental health challenges to improve treatment outcomes. Behavioral aspects of HIV care, including adherence, substance use, and mental health, are critical to ensuring effective management of the disease. The integration of mental health services into HIV care has been explored in various settings, including Uganda, where randomized controlled trials have assessed the feasibility and impact of such interventions. Cost-effectiveness analyses have also demonstrated the value of integrated care models for individuals with HIV, chronic mental illness, and substance use disorders. Global guidelines, such as those from the World Health Organization (WHO), emphasize the importance of differentiated care approaches to address the diverse needs of people living with HIV. These approaches include community-based ART delivery models, which have been shown to reduce the burden on healthcare systems while maintaining high retention rates in care. Examples include community ART groups and distribution points, which reduce travel and waiting times for patients. WHO guidelines also recommend timely linkage to care following an HIV diagnosis. Interventions such as enhanced case management, peer support, and streamlined services have been shown to improve engagement in care and ART initiation. However, challenges such as stigma, transportation costs, and long waiting times remain barriers to effective linkage. In resource-limited settings, less than 30% of individuals diagnosed with HIV navigate the full continuum of care. Retention rates drop significantly over time, with less than 50% of adults remaining in care four years after starting ART. To address these challenges, WHO has introduced operational recommendations to improve service delivery, including task shifting, decentralization, and integration of services. Differentiated care models are particularly important as HIV programs evolve to initiate ART for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of clinical or immunological status. These models cater to the needs of diverse patient groups, including those presenting with advanced disease, those stable on ART, and those requiring close monitoring due to treatment failure or other complications. Community-based ART delivery models have been pioneered in several countries, demonstrating their effectiveness in reducing costs for patients and healthcare systems while maintaining high retention rates. Interventions to improve linkage to care include peer support, navigation approaches, and quality improvement initiatives. These strategies have been shown to increase clinic enrollment and ART initiation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. However, further research is needed to address gaps in evidence and adapt interventions to local contexts. Overall, the integration of HIV care with mental health, NCD management, and community-based delivery models represents a promising approach to improving health outcomes for people living with HIV.
